comments.author: pugio
comments.story_title: The case against conversational interfaces
comments.why_zh: 2013 年用语音写 Python 的精彩演示。
comments.quote_zh: 这让我想起 2013 年那个很棒的 Travis Rudd 用语音写 Python 的视频
comments.text_zh: > 我们需要搞清楚的第二件事，是如何压缩语音输入，让它传输得更快。语音版的点赞或键盘快捷键是什么？我能不能用简单的声音和口哨更快地给 Claude 下提示？这让我想起 2013 年那个很棒的 Travis Rudd 用语音写 Python 的视频：[VIDEO] 过去几年里，我有多少次想要那种“口头快捷键”……很多编程 LLM 的延迟还是稍微有点高，达不到我理想中的心流状态（不过得承认，我还没试过 Groq 之类服务上托管的那些），但我可以清楚地预见到有一天，我会对一个正在跟我聊天、并实时看着我的程序在屏幕上演进的编码模型下达紧凑的指令。说到对话式界面，还有件相关的事：前几天我想学点急救知识，就用 Gemini 把整本教科书读完并生成了 Anki 闪卡，然后把闪卡直接复制粘贴进 ChatGPT 语音模式，让它考我。那大概是我很长一段时间以来最奇妙的语音界面体验了——我可以一边做家务，一边不断被考问我想学的内容，任何时候我有问题或想法，都可以直接让它解释或展开某个术语或某个岔开的话题。
comments.text: > The second thing we need to figure out is how we can compress voice input to make it faster to transmit. What’s the voice equivalent of a thumbs-up or a keyboard shortcut? Can I prompt Claude faster with simple sounds and whistles? This reminds me of the amazing 2013 video of Travis Rudd coding python by voice: [VIDEO] The number of times in the last few years I've wanted that level of "verbal hotkeys"... The latencies of many coding llms are still a little bit too low to allow for my ideal level of flow (though admittedly I haven't tried one's hosted on services like groq), but I can clearly envision a time when I'm issuing tight commands to a coder model that's chatting with me and watching my program evolve on screen in real time. On a somewhat related note to conversational interfaces, the other day I wanted to study some first aid stuff - used Gemini to read the whole textbook and generate Anki flash cards, then copied and pasted the flashcards directly into chat GPT voice mode and had it quiz me. That was probably the most miraculous experience of voice interface I've had in a long time - I could do chores while being constantly quizzed on what I wanted to learn, and anytime I had a question or comment I could just ask it to explain or expound on a term or tangent.

comments.text_zh: 我也有手部问题。我用语音识别来输入所有内容，包括代码，还用游戏手柄来移动鼠标。我现在用的手柄是 PS4 手柄，中间有一块触摸板，所以我能把它贴到脸上蹭，试试她的方法。效果比你想的要好。PS4 的触摸板算不上多出色，但我能移动鼠标、还算准确地点击我想要的东西。当然，手柄上的触摸板很小，也不太精确，所以对画画之类的用途并不太实用。但如果换成一块更好、更大的触摸板，我觉得这方法真的能行。我可能哪天会试试。不过我有点担心免不了的脖子和鼻子疼。我希望她能多讲一点她是怎么避免这个的。也许她就是有钢铁般的脖子？给好奇的人：这些是我找到的一些关于人们应对 RSI 的其他资源。大部分是关于用 Dragon NaturallySpeaking 通过语音编程的，因为那是我最感兴趣的，不过我觉得还是很有意思。真的需要有个地方专门列出针对残障的开源变通方案。据我所知，确实还没有。Natlink + Dragon NaturallySpeaking：（NatLink 让你能用 Python 为 Dragon 制作自定义语音命令，目前正在 [LINK] 开发，但那个网站相当难懂。原作者的网站在 [LINK] 。
comments.text: I also have hand problems. I use speech recognition to type everything, including code, and a game controller to move around the mouse. The controller I'm currently using, a PS4 controller, has a trackpad in the middle, so I was able to mash that against my face and give her technique a shot. It works better than you'd think. The PS4 trackpad isn't exactly brilliant, but I can move around the mouse and click on what I want to with some accuracy. Of course, the trackpad on the controller is very small and not very accurate, so it's not really practical for artwork or anything. But, with a better, larger trackpad, I can imagine this technique actually working. I might give it a shot at some point. I am a bit worried about the inevitable neck and nose pain, though. I wish she had gone into a little more detail about how she avoids that. Maybe she just has a neck of steel? For the curious, these are some other resources I've found about people working around RSI. Most of these are about using Dragon NaturallySpeaking to code by voice, since that's what I'm most interested in, but I think it's still interesting. There really needs to be a list somewhere for open-source workarounds to disabilities. To the best of my knowledge, there really isn't one. Natlink + Dragon NaturallySpeaking: (NatLink, which lets you make custom speech commands for Dragon in Python, is currently being developed at [LINK] , but that site's pretty incomprehensible. The original author's site is at [LINK] .

comments.text: I have been suffering from RSI in both arms for a decade now. It started after coding 10+ hour days working at a game company. The pain ebbs and flows with usage, but the inflammation and tightness has never disappeared completely. Over the years, I've met a number of people who also also suffer from RSI in various forms. Fortunately, the majority of people I talk to suffer for some period of time, but do eventually recover, and are able to continue on with their lives having to be carful to avoid future flareups. A handful though, including myself, seem to fall into the "for life" category. I've tried everything you can think of to varying results: * 15+ doctors in various specialties * Physical therapy * Massage therapists * Chiropractors * Acupuncture * Most every ergonomic keyboard and pointing device on the market * Various desk/chair/keyboard tray ergonomic adjustments * Addressing TMS (See books by Dr. Sarno) * Taking a year off of work (multiple times) * NSAIDs This is resulting in me spending a lot of time looking into other career potabilities, but I keep ending up back writing code to some extent. Voice coding is literally the first thing that comes to everyone's mind when you tell them you have arm pain, but it's a dead end in my mind. I tried to follow in the footsteps of Tavis Rudd, but I just ended up with voice strain from talking too much. You might have better luck though: [VIDEO] At one point in my life, I had an intern who knew how to code type for me. No

comments.text: First, it doesn't feel unpleasant as I do it. There are a few reasons why it might look that way. I have very little practice at this point, especially considering I'm still changing my grammars regularly, so the editing video there is more a technical demo of the software's performance in spite of my own awkwardness while learning. That was my first and only take. I'm basically learning to type again, with cache misses as I try to remember commands and keep track of my position (like trying to remember where keys are, or the next note in a song as you pluck it out). It's also possible the most accurate form of voice input does not sound like natural language. Finally, it's a different mental exercise to copy text that is already written versus writing and editing my own code, so I'm triply out of my element when recording these early videos. comments.text_zh: 我想知道 sub-vocal 会不会很快实现，而即便实现了，我也不确定它能如何解决语音对某些类型的文本来说并非最优的问题。一个例子就是再普通不过的编程，而且需要相当精细的设置。我能找到的最好的例子是 Tavis Rudd 的演讲 [1]，那似乎是个不错的解决方案。我试过或多或少复现这套设置，但发现它不太令人满意。除了要求近乎完美的音频质量才能在一般情况下勉强良好运行（以及初期和持续的大量时间投入）之外，你还经常遇到边缘情况：它就是不想理解你说的某样东西。某个特定短语被误转写第 5 次或第 6 次之后，你往往就放弃了，伸手去拿键盘，RSI 见鬼去吧。（而且这还是作为一个母语为英语、口音相对中性的人。）我完全可以想象，无论是面向编程的语音识别，还是语法本身更适合更轻松、更高效的语音识别的编程语言，都会有更完善的解决方案。如果实现了，我能看到明确的生产力提升。[1] [VIDEO]
comments.text: I wonder if sub-vocal will happen anytime soon, and if it does, I am still not sure how it will solve voice being sub-optimal for some types of text. One example is plain old programming, and needs a fairly elaborate setup. The best example I've been able to find was Tavis Rudd's presentation [1], which seems to be a decent solution. I have tried to more or less replicate this setup, but found it less satisfactory. Aside from it demanding near-perfect audio quality to work remotely well in general (as well as a heavy time investment, initial and ongoing), you frequently run into edge cases where it just doesn't want to understand something you're saying. After the 5th or 6th mis-transcription of some specific phrase, you tend to just give up and reach for the keyboard, RSI be damned. (And this as a native English-speaker, with a relatively neutral accent.) I can definitely imagine better fleshed out solutions to either voice recognition for programming, or programming languages whose syntax lends themselves to easier and more productive voice recognition. I could see some definite productivity enhancements if it were achieved. [1] [VIDEO]
